explanations.answer: A meal with her table set
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Next comes the food: she has prepared her meat, mixed her wine and set her table. She does all of it before a single guest shows up. I've pulled a batch out of the oven with the doorbell already ringing, so a host who's ready ahead of time gets my respect.

No throne in these verses, friend, and no judges either. What Wisdom gets ready is a meal: she has prepared her meat, mixed her wine and set her table. It's a house with dinner waiting. I think that's a much friendlier thing to walk up to than a courtroom.

These verses don't mention an altar. Wisdom prepares her meat, mixes her wine and sets her table. So the next thing in her house is a meal, not an offering. Stick with the table, friend, and you're right on track.

Not quite, friend, because Wisdom doesn't sit still. She has sent out her maidservants, and she calls out from the heights of the city (Proverbs 9:3). That's a host with her own people out spreading the word. I bet the whole neighborhood heard about that dinner.

Right, baker. Wisdom doesn't wait for anyone to stumble on her house. She sends out her maidservants and calls out from the heights of the city (Proverbs 9:3). Her invitation goes out to the people, which is a lot more work than sitting by the door with the lights on.

You've got it, baker. She says, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” and she says it to him who lacks judgment. The invitation goes to the people who don't have it all figured out yet. I qualify on a good day, and the door is open to me too.

Good thought, but her words go somewhere else. She says, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” and she says it to him who lacks judgment (Proverbs 9:4). The simple are the ones she's calling. The wise do show up later in the passage, so hang on to that.

No priests in this invitation, friend. She calls to the simple, saying, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” and she says it to him who lacks judgment. The passage doesn't name any temple crowd. Her call is for anyone who is simple and willing to turn in.

Yes, baker. She says, “Leave your folly behind, and you will live; walk in the way of understanding.” The only thing she asks you to drop at the door is the folly. Bring your appetite and leave that at home. I once tried to carry too many trays at once, and believe me, putting something down is sometimes the smartest move.

Her invitation never mentions money, friend. What she says is, “Leave your folly behind, and you will live; walk in the way of understanding.” (Proverbs 9:6) The one thing to leave at the door is folly. Your wallet can stay in your pocket.

No weapons come up here, baker. Wisdom says, “Leave your folly behind, and you will live; walk in the way of understanding.” The thing to leave behind is folly. It sounds like a much lighter bag to carry.

That's the word, baker. She says, “Leave your folly behind, and you will live…” Her invitation comes with a promise of life. A host who sets a table and then promises life to the guests, that's a good invitation.

Close in sound but not in meaning, friend. She says, “Leave your folly behind, and you will live…” The promise is life, not wandering. Walking in the way of understanding is the opposite of drifting around lost.

That's not what she promises, baker. Her words are, “Leave your folly behind, and you will live…” Wisdom's invitation points toward life. If anything, the suffering is what the passage ties to the other road later on.

Yes, baker. The passage says, “He who corrects a mocker brings shame on himself…” Correcting a mocker doesn't earn you a thank-you. It costs you. Sometimes the kindest move is to save your breath and keep your own apron clean.

I wish it worked that way, friend. The very next verse says, “Do not rebuke a mocker, or he will hate you…” (Proverbs 9:8). So respect isn't what comes back. The verse before it says the one who corrects a mocker brings shame on himself.

explanations.answer: He earns praise from the elders
explanations.explanation: The elders don't show up in this verse, baker. It says, “He who corrects a mocker brings shame on himself…” So the one who steps up gets shame, not applause. I think that's a hard lesson, but it's a clear one.

That's right, baker. The passage says, “…rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.” (Proverbs 9:8) A wise man takes the correction and thanks you for it. Compare that with the mocker, who hates you for it. It's a good reminder to be the wise one when a correction comes my way.

It's actually true, friend. The text says, “…rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.” The mocker hates the rebuke, but the wise man loves the one who gives it. That's the difference between the two of them in this verse.
You got it, baker. The passage says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom…” That's where wisdom starts. Not at the end of a long climb, but at the very first step.

Study is a fine thing, friend, but that's not what this verse names. It says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom…” Wisdom begins there, before the years of learning pile up. Starting at the right place matters more than how long you've been going.

Kings don't appear in this verse, baker. It says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom…” That's the starting point the passage gives. It's not advice from the powerful, it's the fear of the LORD.

That's the word, baker. The passage says, “For through wisdom your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life.” Days multiplied and years added, it's a double promise. I'll take extra time in the bakery any day.

Not servants, friend. The verse says, “For through wisdom your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life.” What gets added is years, not people to wait on you. The gift here is time.

No battles in this promise, baker. The verse says, “For through wisdom your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life.” What wisdom adds is years. It's a promise about life, not about fights.
Yes, baker. The first blank is wise: “If you are wise, you are wise to your own advantage…” The benefit lands right on the one who chooses wisdom. It's like a good batch you get to eat yourself.

That's the second blank, friend. The verse says, “…but if you scoff, you alone will bear the consequences.” The word is scoff, and the weight lands on the scoffer alone. Nobody else gets handed that bill.
Riches don't come up in this verse, baker. It says, “If you are wise, you are wise to your own advantage…” The word that fits is wise. Being wise pays off for you, whatever's in your pocket.

Rest is a nice idea, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The text says, “…but if you scoff, you alone will bear the consequences.” Scoff is the word that fits the second blank. Resting won't do anything about those consequences.

Waiting doesn't fit here, baker. The verse says, “If you are wise, you are wise to your own advantage; but if you scoff, you alone will bear the consequences.” The words are wise and scoff. Nobody gets to wait it out, because the consequences are real.

That's right, baker. The passage says, “She sits at the door of her house…” (Proverbs 9:14). Folly has her own house, just like Wisdom. Both women have a place and both are calling people to it. That's what makes this choice a tricky one.

She does have one, friend. The passage says Folly sits at the door of her house, on a seat in the heights of the city (Proverbs 9:14). So she and Wisdom both have a house and both call out from the heights. Two houses, two invitations.

Yes, baker. Folly says, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” and Wisdom said those same words in Proverbs 9:4. They're an exact match. I think that's what makes her so tricky, because she sounds just like the other invitation.

Surprise, friend: she doesn't open with opposite words. Folly says, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” That's exactly what Wisdom said in Proverbs 9:4. The two invitations start the very same way.
Not softer, baker. Folly says, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” and Wisdom used those same words in Proverbs 9:4. The opening line is an exact match. The difference comes after it.

explanations.answer: Bread eaten in secret is tasty
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Folly says, “Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is tasty!” Notice how the pitch leans on secrecy and stealing. It sounds exciting, but the verse right after tells the rest.

explanations.answer: Bread bought at market is cheap
explanations.explanation: No market in her pitch, friend. Folly says, “Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is tasty!” Her bread is tasty because it's eaten in secret. Price never comes up.

explanations.answer: Bread shared with friends is best
explanations.explanation: Folly says nearly the opposite, baker. Her words are, “Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is tasty!” Her pitch is about secret bread, not shared bread. A bakery full of friends sounds better to me.

Yes, baker, and it's a heavy one. The passage says the dead are there, and that her guests are in the depths of Sheol (Proverbs 9:18). Her pitch sounds sweet and tasty, but that's what's inside. I think this is a serious line, and it's worth sitting with.

That's how she makes it sound, friend, but it isn't what's there. The passage says the dead are there, and that her guests are in the depths of Sheol (Proverbs 9:18). It's a heavy verse. Her pitch is sweet and the truth is not.

No treasure in that house, baker. The passage says the dead are there, and that her guests are in the depths of Sheol (Proverbs 9:18). It's a heavy line. The pitch sounds tasty, but the verse tells what's really inside.

Not quite, friend. The passage says, “But they do not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.” They don't know. That's the trouble with her pitch, because the people walking in can't see what's inside.

Right, baker. The passage says, “But they do not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.” The ones she invites don't know. It's a heavy verse, and it shows why Wisdom's call matters.
